\section[\hi{हरा}]{\hi{हरा} — a color cousin hiding in plain sight}

\label{lesson:HI-C24-hara-pila}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Hindi's green word shares deep roots with words other languages use for yellow.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{हरा} — a hidden cousin of jaune and gelb}
\textbf{\hi{हरा}} (\textbf{harā}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{green}\textquotedblright{}) comes from \textbf{Sanskrit} \textbf{\hi{हरित}} (\textbf{harita}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{green, yellowish, tawny}\textquotedblright{}) — a well-documented descendant of \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{*ǵ\textsuperscript{h}elh\textsubscript{3}-}}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to shine}.\textquotedblright{} That confirmed root is also behind \textbf{German}'s \textbf{gelb} (via Proto-Germanic \emph{*gelwaz}) and English's own \textquotedblleft{}yellow\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}gold\textquotedblright{} — making Hindi's word for \textbf{GREEN} a genuine cousin of German's word for \textbf{YELLOW}. \textbf{French}'s \textbf{jaune} is usually traced to this same family too, via Latin \emph{galbinus} — though, honestly, that particular link is \textbf{less secure} than the others: some modern Latin scholarship treats \emph{galbus}'s origin as unknown rather than confirming the \emph{*ǵ\textsuperscript{h}elh\textsubscript{3}-} connection. So here's the honest surprise: Hindi's word for GREEN and German's word for YELLOW are, at the deepest level, \textbf{cousins} — not a contradiction, since this root originally covered a blurry \textquotedblleft{}shining, yellow-to-green\textquotedblright{} zone before languages carved out different pieces of it. Sanskrit \emph{harita} itself kept some of that blur, historically covering shades from green through yellowish and tawny, before Hindi's \emph{harā} settled specifically on \textquotedblleft{}green.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}

  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}\hi{हरा}\textquotedblright{} — green, a hidden PIE cousin of German's gelb{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}\emph{ǵ\textsuperscript{h}elh\textsubscript{3}-} — shine, then a yellow-to-green color zone\textquotedblright{}{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What ancient Proto-Indo-European root connects \textbf{harā} to German's \emph{gelb}? (\emph{\textbf{*ǵ\textsuperscript{h}elh\textsubscript{3}-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to shine\textquotedblright{} — Hindi's GREEN word is a genuine cousin of German's YELLOW word; French's \emph{jaune} is usually placed in this family too, though that link is less secure.) Why can one root yield green and yellow words? (It once covered a broader \textbf{shining yellow-to-green zone}.) Next: the yellow word whose sound history is clear but meaning history is not.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pīlā]{\hi{पीला} — clear sounds, uncertain meaning}

\label{lesson:HI-C24-pila-history}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} \emph{Harā} gave a secure ancient color family. Hindi's yellow word gives a secure sound chain wrapped around an unsolved semantic mystery.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The chain}
\textbf{\hi{पीला}} (\emph{pīlā}, \textquotedblleft{}yellow\textquotedblright{}) traces through Prakrit \textbf{\hi{पीअल}} (\emph{pīala}) to Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{पीतल}} (\emph{pītala}), built on \textbf{\hi{पीत}} (\emph{pīta}).

\emph{Pīta} means \textquotedblleft{}yellow,\textquotedblright{} but also literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}drunk, quaffed,\textquotedblright{}} from a root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to drink.\textquotedblright{} Why do \textquotedblleft{}yellow\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}drunk\textquotedblright{} share a word? The connection is \textbf{not settled}. One proposed path runs \textquotedblleft{}drink\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}become full or swell\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}the color of fat\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}yellow,\textquotedblright{} but sources flag that mechanism as uncertain.

What is solid is the ordinary sound history:

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{pīta\emph{ $\to$ }pītala\emph{ $\to$ }pīala\emph{ $\to$ }pīlā}}
\end{quote}

Keep the evidence levels separate: trust the forms; label the semantic bridge a hypothesis.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}pīlā\textquotedblright{} — yellow{]}
  \item {[}YOU TRACE: \textquotedblleft{}pīta · pītala · pīala · pīlā\textquotedblright{}{]}
  \item {[}YOU QUALIFY: \textquotedblleft{}drink $\to$ yellow is uncertain\textquotedblright{}{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{pīta} also mean? (\textbf{Drunk, quaffed}.) Is the bridge from drinking to yellow settled? (\textbf{No}.) What part is secure? (The sound chain \emph{pīta} $\to$ \emph{pītala} $\to$ \emph{pīala} $\to$ \emph{pīlā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
